title: AssoMem: Scalable Memory QA with Multi-Signal Associative Retrieval
claim: Retrieval based only on semantic relevance returns plausible but wrong items; our multi-signal method recovers the evidence and beats baselines across benchmarks.
layout: 3 regions: questions and failures left, memory base right, bar chart below
description: The top half is a failure-case illustration. On the left, two rounded boxes hold example questions (Q1 about work complaints, Q2 about which show was watched first). Below them are two 'Top-1 Retrieval' boxes. Each contains an utterance tagged with a pink 'Error' label. A bold caption reads 'Relevance solely is insufficient for retrieval'. On the right, a large 'Memory Base' box lists dialogue utterances. Green 'Evidence' tags mark the correct ones, and pink 'Error' tags mark the distractors that look similar to the query. The bottom half is a grouped bar chart of Recall@6 on MeetingQA, LongMemeval_m and LongMemeval_l. It compares four methods, with AssoMem in purple as the tallest bar in every group. The eye goes first to the colored tags, then to the bars.
caption: An example showing limitations in relevance solely retrieval. Our \method\ consistently outperforms SOTA baselines on three datasets.
abstract: Accurate recall from large scale memories remains a core challenge for memory augmented AI assistants performing question answering (QA), especially in similarity dense scenarios where existing methods mainly rely on semantic distance to the query for retrieval. Inspired by how humans link information associatively, we propose AssoMem, a novel framework constructing an associative memory graph that anchors dialogue utterances to automatically extracted clues. This structure provides a rich organizational view of the conversational context and facilitates importance aware ranking. Further, AssoMem integrates multi-dimensional retrieval signals-relevance, importance, and temporal alignment using an adaptive mutual information (MI) driven fusion strategy. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks and a newly introduced dataset, MeetingQA, demonstrate that AssoMem consistently outperforms SOTA baselines, verifying its superiority in context-aware memory recall.
